old_title: COP31: UN Climate summit runs long with no deal in sight after fossil fuels omitted from draft
new_title: COP31: Climate deal 'not adopted' as EU, others reject draft declaration over fossil fuels omission
old_text:
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- A new draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'
- Like in previous years, the climate summit has been extended until a consensus is reached
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 and Saturday, November 21:
Peru blames 'geopolitical divisions' for lack of COP31 progress
The head of Peru's delegation at COP31, Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, warned that the UN climate summit was unlikely to end with a concrete deal on climate financing or cutting fossil fuel use.
Garrido Sanchez lamented that the outcome "would be very limited."
He reiterated how "geopolitical divisions" were stopping any final deal from mentioning reducing reliance on oil, gas and coal.
The Peruvian delegate singled out major oil producers, such as Gulf Arab states and Russia, as showing significant opposition.
He noted that while Latin American neighbor Panama had also signaled objection to including the term fossil fuels in the final text, Peru was "not so radical" and is keen to attract investment to "ensure our energy security" through renewables.
China throws weight behind '35-by-35' pledge
China has backed a plan proposed by COP host Turkey to raise global electricity demand to 35% by 2035 - up from the current 20%.
In a joint statement with Australia, which is leading negotiations between almost 200 nations at the COP31 summit in Turkey, Beijing said it welcomes "growing international ambition and cooperation ... to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 on a voluntary basis."
The statement goes on to highlight the benefits the transition can bring for the economy, jobs, energy security, public health and households.
The two partners also "acknowledge the importance of inclusive climate action that ensures no one is left behind," the text continued.
Dozens of countries, including EU states, Japan, South Korea and Canada, have so far signaled support for the voluntary goal, which aims to boost clean energy use.
Yet, environmental groups have warned that the draft text doesn't stipulate the use of solar, wind and other renewable energy sources, which could allow power plants using natural gas and coal to be included.
COP31: What to expect today
Good morning, and welcome back to DW's coverage of the UN's COP31 climate summit in Turkey.
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries worked through the night to finalize a deal, after a draft text dropped all mention of fossil fuels - the leading cause of climate change.
COP31, being held in the Mediterranean city of Antalya, was due to wrap up on Friday, but has run over time amid deep divisions over fossil fuels.
Hopes are fading that negotiators will finalize concrete plans to drastically slash the use of oil, gas and coal and a deeper commitment to renewable energy.
Stay tuned as we bring you the latest from the closing stages of UN climate summit.
COP31 talks go on - we're taking a break
The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, has gone into overtime, with countries still divided over key issues, including fossil fuels and climate financing.
The talks were scheduled to end on Friday evening, but negotiators have yet to reach an agreement. Germany and several other countries are pushing for a clear commitment to phase out fossil fuels, while poorer nations are demanding more concrete financial support to cope with climate change.
Negotiations are expected to continue into the weekend. We are pausing our live coverage for now and will bring you further updates as talks progress.
WATCH - Turkey's beaches are becoming too hot for sea turtles
While Turkey hosts COP31 in Antalya, a growing climate threat is unfolding on its Mediterranean beaches. Rising sand temperatures are causing most newly hatched sea turtles to be born female, raising concerns about the long-term survival of local populations.
Conservationists warn that climate change, combined with pollution, coastal development and fishing-related injuries, is putting increasing pressure on the species.
DW correspondent Julia Hahn follows the people working to protect Turkey's iconic loggerhead turtles and shows how the climate crisis is already affecting wildlife far beyond the COP31 conference halls.
WATCH - COP climate summit under scrutiny over fossil fuel influence
The UN climate summit in Antalya is drawing criticism from activists and campaigners who question whether global climate talks can deliver meaningful change while fossil fuel interests remain influential. Turkey and Australia, both under scrutiny for their energy policies, are leading this year's conference.
Activists, including Greta Thunberg, argue COP summits have become increasingly ineffective, while others defend them as a vital space to pressure governments. Climate policy experts say the talks have helped reduce projected warming, but stress that real progress depends on action taken by countries between summits, not just agreements reached at them.
WATCH - Maldives environment minister: 'We are not going to live in the dark'
For the Maldives, climate change is already affecting everyday life. Heavy rainfall has forced people from their homes, warmer oceans are damaging coral reefs, and changes in fish stocks are putting pressure on the country's fishing industry. Rising sea levels pose another threat to the low-lying island nation. Meanwhile, global greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise, despite more than three decades of international climate negotiations.
At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, the Maldives' climate minister Ali Sharif discusses why progress has been so slow, what really happens during climate negotiations, and why moving away from fossil fuels is not as straightforward as it might seem.
For island nations like the Maldives, switching to renewable energy comes with practical and financial challenges. So what would it take to accelerate the transition? And can the UN climate process still deliver meaningful results?
COP32 hosts Ethiopia call the conferences a relay, not a single race
The hosts of next year's COP, Ethiopia, found a nationally tailored sporting metaphor to sum up the difficult, ongoing, sometimes tortuous process that the global environmental meetings can prove to be.
Speaking at the end of Friday's plenary to confirm Addis Ababa's intentions to host next year's summit, Gedion Timothewos, the foreign minister and upcoming president of COP32, made reference to Ethiopia's longstanding success in endurance running in track and field.
Referring to the COP process as a marathon, not a sprint, Timothewos said the country was looking forward to picking up the baton from Turkey and leading the next leg of the relay, taking the ongoing process forward into 2027.
His comments came during a late-night plenary session, but more talks are still expected in Antalya.
Late-night plenary session convenes after delay
Shortly after 9 p.m. local time in Antalya, delegates gathered for a plenary session, well past the official closing time.
The Turkish presidency's opening address was partly drowned out by a protester shouting objections in English such as "you are killing the future," and gaining applause within the chamber.
"We've been negotiating for days to find the common ground," COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, told the plenary. He hailed the progress made and said the world "waits for good news from this room."
But the plenary session noted how several of the more ambitious aspects of a political declaration remained incomplete, with no agreement yet reached at the summit.
Several national delegates spoke during the plenary to bemoan the elusive progress or even backsliding during the two weeks of negotiations.
The evening's session, however, has been dealing with technical issues, and the possibility that discussions continue into the weekend remains.
IN DEPTH - Climate science disputes and disinformation hinder action at COP
Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?
The UN's IPCC should have already started work on its next series of multi-year scientific assessments on climate change's progress, but the process is on hold at the urging of countries including fossil fuel-producing giants Russia, Saudi Arabia and Iran.
Read Tim Schauenberg's full report on this obstruction to climate research and other similar issues complicating COP31 here.
IN DEPTH - US is strong at climate talks despite Trump no-show
The US government is snubbing UN climate talks in Turkey. That's prompted a delegation of American lawmakers, mayors and governors to make the trip instead, aiming to show that climate action in the US is alive and well.
Head over to this report to learn more about who is representing the US at the summit, even if President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly dismissed global warming as a "hoax", didn't send a formal delegation for the second year in a row.
IN DEPTH - Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.
Learn more about what Uganda's environment minister Beatrice Atim Anywar said about climate financing in this report.
Activist Menotti: Europe has 'learned a few of the Trump tactics'
Veteran climate justice advocate Victor Menotti of the Demand Climate Justice NGO told DW that European governments appeared to be copying US President Donald Trump's negotiating playbook at COP this year.
"We know the US isn't here, but we can see that Germany and other European governments have learned a few of the Trump tactics, maybe in the trade disputes with the US," Menotti said. "And we see them applying here in Antalya, where it's like: Don't admit to anything. Try to dilute your responsibilities. Weaken whatever obligations you have. And then take even more."
He argued these countries were also expecting unreasonable or unfeasible commitments from developing countries, for instance restrictions on what they can spend money on and obligations to report on their expenditures.
"Germany is subsidizing quite a bit of coal still and fossil fuels, LNG expansion infrastructure," he said, arguing that wealthier countries' energy spending also had room for improvement.
"We need the North to act first," Menotti said. "The deal from Paris, the deal from Rio 30 years ago, is that the North will lead. But yet we see too much bullying of the global South and not enough leadership like they agreed to."
Talks formally enter overtime as scheduled close elapses
You can cross off another box on your COP31 bingo cards, dear readers.
As of the top of this hour, the session has officially gone past its scheduled end time of 1500 GMT/UTC on Friday, or 6 p.m. local time on site in Turkey.
This is something of an annual tradition at COP summits, which are always scheduled to finish at the end of a working week but also almost invariably run into the closing weekend. Delegates and members of the media tend to book their travel plans with this in mind.
'Electrification': What to know about the revised draft declaration
The revised draft declaration, which critics have slammed as "watered down" due to the omission of fossil fuels, highlights the "electrification" of the global economy as a central pillar of the energy transition.
"Electrification is the key to transitioning away from fossil fuels," Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen told reporters.
What are the key points to know about the "35-by-35" electrification target?
- The draft wants to increase electricity's share of global energy use from 23% to 35% by 2035
- The draft highlights electrification as a way to cut emissions and boost energy security - while omitting prior mentions of fossil fuels
- It aims to shift more transport, heating, cooling and industrial activity onto electricity, allowing those sectors to be powered by renewables such as wind, solar and hydro power, rather than by burning coal, oil or gas
But the text does not specify what energy sources would supply the electricity. Some countries are demanding that the text call for "clean" electrification to clearly favor renewable sources over coal, oil or gas.
Bowen, who has been trying to secure compromises, pledged to continue working over the "coming hours, for as long as it takes, to get the job done."
"People have strong views of course - I am not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me let's give up and go home," Bowen said.
new_text:
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- The summit's president acknowledges that a deal was 'not adopted'
- The final declaration omits any mention of fossil fuels
- The EU says it cannot accept a deal that 'greenwashes fossil fuels'
- Fossil fuels are a major flashpoint at this year's summit, which comes amid soaring energy prices and tensions over the US-Israeli war with Iran
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 through Sunday, November 22:
COP31 fails to agree climate deal amid fossil fuel rift
The COP31 climate summit has failed to agree on a final joint declaration.
During a plenary session, the summit's Turkish president acknowledged there would be no climate deal.
"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey's environment minister, told a closing plenary in the Mediterranean city of Antalya.
The rift centered on whether to include the phaseout of fossil fuels in the final declaration. Scientists say the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas is the main cause of global warming.
European nations, smaller island states and climate activists have criticized oil-producing countries for the omission.
Ghana says COP presidency has not 'shown respect'
Several nations continued to raise serious objections to the draft.
Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, took a shot at the presidency for how it has handled the negotiations.
"With all due respect Mr. President, you have not shown respect to a group of 54 countries (from Africa) and my country (Ghana) for that matter," Amoah said.
Panama rejects draft decision, saying it 'should be based on science'
Panama's representative said the Central American nation was amongst those who suffer most from the consequences and issue of climate justice.
Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks were being held hostage by a "petroleum mafia" and need to be reformed.
He said science must be the basis for the cover decision, adding that those who contributed to this crisis must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it.
"We are running out of time," Navarro told attendees. "Panama cannot support this decision. The planet cannot continue to wait."
EU cannot accept deal that 'greenwashes fossil fuels': Irish minister
Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O'Brien has said the European Union is "profoundly disappointed" with the current draft deal on the table at COP31 because it "fails to meet the moment" and that the bloc will not agree to it.
"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5°C within reach," O'Brien said.
"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time. And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels," he added.
Former Greenpeace chief says no deal is better than current deal
Former Greenpeace executive Jennifer Morgan said it would be better to end the COP31 summit with no deal than a watered-down declaration.
Her remarks come amid deep divisions over the omission of fossil fuels from the draft declaration.
Morgan rejected the notion that it would be better to accept the current draft than have no resolution at all, as the Turkish COP president has suggested.
"I think this is the day for the first time in my 31 COPs that I thought it was better not to have a decision that sets us back, that goes against what small islands and vulnerable people are saying," Morgan added.
She praised Germany for standing up to pressures to accept the current deal.
"Of course it would have been better to have a strong outcome here with everyone moving forward, but I agree with the German minister who just said if the text stays the way that it is, then it should not be accepted," Morgan said.
The US climate activist blamed oil-producing nations for the impasse.
"Saudi Arabia's fingerprints are all over" the current draft proposal, she said.
The omission has created a deadlock at COP31, which was due to conclude on Friday but has been extended as delegates seek consensus.
Morgan also blamed this year's Turkish presidency for failing to bring everybody together and instead letting countries that rely on fossil fuels dictate the terms of the agreement.
"Last year we had Brazil with a very strong presidency. They worked all year to bring countries together and they managed. It was not easy last year," Morgan said.
"This year we had presidencies that, in my view, were not well prepared. They did not bring countries together (...) it's been shuttle diplomacy with no text for four days. That's not the way you get an agreement here," she added.
Germany rejects 'unacceptable' draft deal
German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider has said the latest version of the draft agreement is "not acceptable."
Schneider said that the draft decision "not only fails to provide an adequate response but actually takes a step backward. A step backward from previous decisions on climate protection is the last thing Germany can support."
Schneider said that delegates had been working hard for days to reach a unanimous decision on "the world's greatest challenge: human-induced climate change," noting that this summer had "shown that the nature of this warming not only costs lives - as in Nepal - but also changes our world for the worse."
"It is up to us, as humanity, to do something about it. That is why a conference dedicated to climate protection - whose sole purpose is to protect the climate - must send a clear signal that we are taking action against this threat."
Schneider said he still believed most nations are willing to work to enact climate protection, but singled out those who still rely on fossil fuels to power their economies.
"The overwhelming majority of nations are committed to climate protection. Some, however, are still making huge profits from oil and gas and are unwilling to scale back their production or to pioneer a clear roadmap for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in this area," he added.
France criticizes draft deal as 'backward' step
France has called a new draft deal proposed at COP31 a "backward" step.
French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut criticized the deal for failing to mention fossil fuels, casting fresh uncertainty over whether nations will be able to reach an agreement.
"Time is ticking and we are not there yet," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said in a statement.
Turkish COP31 president calls for resolution to be adopted
COP31 President Murat Kurum has expressed his frustration over the deadlock at the summit.
The latest version of the draft deal again fails to mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Over 40 hours after its scheduled conclusion and with no compromise in sight, the summit risks losing the numbers required to make any decision as delegates leave for home.
"If it is not adopted, I believe those who push the COP process into a deadlock will need to reflect on their position," Kurum said.
"It is our wish that this resolution be passed. We shall shortly be expressing our determination to ensure that this resolution is passed at the general meeting," he said.
"It is up to the parties involved. If there is sincerity here, and if there is a genuine desire to get things done, I believe that this can be achieved in this chamber. We shall see about that in a moment," Kurum added.
What we know about the latest COP31 draft deal
The third draft makes no mention of the words "fossil," "oil," "coal," or "phase out."
However, as in the second draft, the latest version retains a goal to boost electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, as well as efforts to expand the use of "clean energy."
The draft text also does not stipulate that the "35-by-35" electrification target should be met using renewable energy sources.
It also urges countries to "accelerate" carbon capture and storage - a controversial technology backed by the fossil fuel industry.
Fossil fuels still missing in latest COP31 draft deal
Welcome back to our coverage of the UN's COP31 climate summit in Turkey.
The latest, and potentially final, version of the deal still makes no explicit mention of fossil fuels.
It does refer to a 2023 agreement that committed the world to transitioning away from fossil fuels - but stops short of naming them directly.
The third and presumably final draft text to emerge from negotiations at COP31, which lacks any mention of fossil fuels or how to transition away from them, has been rejected by NGOs.
In a statement, Teresa Anderson, Climate Justice Lead at ActionAid International, said the people who will benefit most from the new "35-by-35" electrification targets and carbon capture "are the fossil fuel, nuclear, data and CCUS (carbon capture, use and storage) industries.
"This text will help elites to profit while leaving people in the dark," Anderson said.
Brandon Wu, AAUSA's Director of Policy and Campaigns, said: "Rich countries came to the COP31 talks with nothing to offer other than red lines.
"They put forward meaningless fossil fuel transition roadmaps that were nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy, then hypocritically blamed developing countries for failing to take action on phasing out fossil fuels.
"This is the behaviour of an arrogant bully who cares about nothing but himself and it is no way to have a proper negotiation. COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise."
We're pausing our coverage
As COP31 extends into a second day of overtime, we are pausing our coverage.
In the early hours of Sunday, COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum informed delegates at a plenary that a third and "final" text would be sent to them for review.
He added that negotiators would have until 6:00 am (0400 GMT) "to come to us with agreement on the text" and that a closing plenary would then be convened at 9:00 am local time.
Stay tuned for more news in the coming hours.
IN DEPTH: Why electrification is the climate game changer we need
The shift to green tech is already in full swing, including electric cars, electric buses, solar panels and heat pumps. But what is so electrifying about the latest wave of electrification?
Climate activist blames rich countries for COP failure
Harjeet Singh, the global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign and strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, said that COP31 could be a failure due to a lack of funding.
"COP31 is stuck for one simple reason: money. Europe and other rich countries came to Antalya with empty pockets," he wrote in a statement shared with multiple reporters.
"They've spent two weeks pushing electrification targets and demanding more ambition from developing countries, while refusing to pay for any of it," he added.
Singh accused wealthy countries of blocking a just transition mechanism and of ignoring calls to increase funding for the Adaptation Fund and the Loss and Damage Fund.
"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he wrote.
The climate activist stressed that the reason this COP failed wasn't a lack of solutions. It was due to "a lack of money and a lack of will from those who caused this crisis," he said.
IN DEPTH: Why is carbon capture not moving faster?
Carbon capture technology works, but its real-world capabilities are nowhere near to moving the needle on climate change. So what's the hold-up?
IN DEPTH: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
Attacks on climate science and disinformation seem to be delaying key decisions as the UN climate talks draw to a close in Antalya.

"We know the US isn't here, but we can see that Germany and other European governments have learned a few of the Trump tactics, maybe in the trade disputes with the US," Menotti said. "And we see them applying here in Antalya, where it's like: Don't admit to anything. Try to dilute your responsibilities. Weaken whatever obligations you have. And then take even more." He argued these countries were also expecting unreasonable or unfeasible commitments from developing countries, for instance restrictions on what they can spend money on and obligations to report on their expenditures. "Germany is subsidizing quite a bit of coal still and fossil fuels, LNG expansion infrastructure," he said, arguing that wealthier countries' energy spending also had room for improvement. "We need the North to act first," Menotti said. "The deal from Paris, the deal from Rio 30 years ago, is that the North will lead. 'Electrification': What to know about the revised draft declaration The revised draft declaration, which critics have slammed as "watered down" due to the omission of fossil fuels, highlights the "electrification" of the global economy as a central pillar of the energy transition. "Electrification is the key to transitioning away from fossil fuels," Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen told reporters. What are the key points to know about the "35-by-35" electrification target? - The draft wants to increase electricity's share of global energy use from 23% to 35% by 2035 - The draft highlights electrification as a way to cut emissions and boost energy security - while omitting prior mentions of fossil fuels - It aims to shift more transport, heating, cooling and industrial activity onto electricity, allowing those sectors to be powered by renewables such as wind, solar and hydro power, rather than by burning coal, oil or gas But the text does not specify what energy sources would supply the electricity. Some countries are demanding that the text call for "clean" electrification to clearly favor renewable sources over coal, oil or gas. Bowen, who has been trying to secure compromises, pledged to continue working over the "coming hours, for as long as it takes, to get the job done." "People have strong views of course - I am not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me let's give up and go home," Bowen said.
